sentence: Erectile dysfunction is the persistent inability to get or keep an erection.
Erectile dysfunction, also called impotence, means being unable to get or keep an erection.
Occasional problems are common and are often linked to stress, tiredness or heavy drinking.
When the problem keeps happening, the NHS says it can point to conditions such as high blood pressure, high cholesterol, diabetes, depression or anxiety, or hormone problems.
Treatment includes medicines called PDE-5 inhibitors, counselling and treatment of any underlying condition.

sentence: NHS inform adds that people are advised to contact their GP practice when symptoms have lasted more than a few months, self-help has not worked and the problem is bothering them.
The NHS says some medicines can cause erection problems as a side effect.
Long-term conditions can also play a part, including high blood pressure, high cholesterol and diabetes.
Mental health matters too, because the NHS lists depression and anxiety among the possible causes.
Hormone problems are another cause the NHS mentions.
The Sexual Advice Association explains that erection problems that only happen with a partner can still have a physical cause.
For that reason, it says a check with a GP comes first.
If the physical checks come back clear, it says psychological causes may be involved.
It gives performance pressure, anxiety and feelings about the partner or relationship as examples.
Heavy drinking is one of the everyday reasons the NHS gives for occasional problems.
The Sexual Advice Association says erection problems can be an early sign of heart disease.
It also says they can be associated with diabetes.
The British Heart Foundation says erectile dysfunction can signal atherosclerosis, which is a build-up of fatty material in the arteries.
It says atherosclerosis raises the risk of a heart attack and stroke.
The same charity notes that the arteries of the penis are narrow, so problems there can appear among the first warning signs.
MedlinePlus, a US health resource, also describes erectile dysfunction as an early indicator of a higher risk of atherosclerosis.
It says men with erection problems can raise plaque build-up with their health care provider.
For these reasons, the Sexual Advice Association says a thorough check by a GP matters.
A clinician will usually ask about lifestyle and relationships, check blood pressure and examine the genitals.
Depending on what is found, the clinician may refer the person for further tests.
The Sexual Advice Association says a GP check is the first step, so that physical causes can be looked for.
Prescribing guidance from one NHS area says psychosexual causes should be explored.
It also says medicines that may cause erection problems should be considered.
The same guidance says men who already have cardiovascular disease are assessed before a PDE-5 inhibitor is prescribed.
The NHS says a GP or a sexual health clinic is the place to go when erection problems keep happening.

sentence: The NHS says the main treatments are medicines called PDE-5 inhibitors, which increase blood flow to the penis.

sentence: The NHS names sildenafil, tadalafil, vardenafil and avanafil as examples.
A NICE evidence summary says that first-line treatment is usually an oral PDE-5 inhibitor.
Prescribing guidance from one NHS area adds that these medicines do not start an erection by themselves but need sexual stimulation.
The NHS says sildenafil can be bought from a pharmacy, and it advises seeing a doctor before buying medicines online.
Treating an underlying condition is another approach.
Counselling can help when emotional or mental health factors are involved.
One NHS page notes that there can be a long wait for counselling services on the NHS.
Vacuum pumps can be used when medicine is not suitable or does not work, though they are not always available on the NHS.
The NHS lists lifestyle changes that can help, including stopping smoking, eating a healthy diet and exercising.
Local NHS guidance also lists weight loss and reducing alcohol.
The Sexual Advice Association suggests slowing things down with a partner and focusing on closeness rather than erections for a period.
It also says partners can talk through any sexual issues together.
It describes sex therapy as a talking therapy.
It says a GP or another NHS health professional may be able to refer someone for sex therapy, depending on the area.
Sex therapy can also be arranged by contacting a therapist directly and paying privately.
If problems continue, it suggests a sex therapist.
A painful erection that lasts a long time is called priapism.
The NHS says a prolonged erection needs care at A&E because of the risk of permanent damage.
NHS 111 Wales says a person with this problem should not drive themselves, and that someone else can drive or 999 can be called.
Priapism most commonly affects people with sickle cell disease.
Other causes include blood-thinning medicines such as warfarin, some antidepressants and some treatments for erectile dysfunction.
NHS 111 Wales gives a shorter time limit than the NHS priapism page, so the length of time that counts as an emergency differs between sources.
